title: What the UK Owes to Yemen
guest_line: Asst. Professor of International Relations, University of Sussex · author of AngloArabia: Why Gulf Wealth Matters to Britain
report: Report: Reparations for Yemen (CAAT & Transition Security Project, Sept 2026), with Sam Perlo-Freeman & Khem Rogaly
thesis: Britain enabled one of the most devastating wars of the modern era. It owes Yemen reparations, not charity.
footer: Mind map built from a machine transcript of the episode audio. Figures checked against the CAAT/TSP report. Timestamps refer to the episode.

leaves.x: Yemen is Saudi Arabia’s “backyard”: strategic real estate on the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the foot of the Red Sea. Riyadh, and the West, want a friendly government there.
The 2011 Arab uprising topples the government, but no stable successor emerges and rival factions compete for power.
Ansar Allah (the Houthis), a rebel movement from the north, take the capital and the populous north and west.
Saudi-led intervention to restore the “internationally recognised government”: recognised abroad, with a thin social base at home.
The UAE is the other regional power. On the ground the coalition is a disparate, unwieldy mix of government loyalists, southern separatists and militias.
a war of attrition, then a grinding stalemate
2022: the UAE gives up and the Saudis lose faith. A “cold peace” follows until 2026, when Ansar Allah and Saudi Arabia escalate once more.

branches.title: Britain’s Role
branches.sub: Every practical way short of combat

leaves.x: An aerial war: Yemeni militias on the ground, with air cover from the Royal Saudi Air Force, whose aircraft are roughly half British and half American.
Thatcher’s mega-deal for Tornado jets and Hawk trainers. More Tornados followed under Major (early 1990s), then Typhoons under New Labour (late 2000s).
A jet sale is a relationship, not a transaction: training jets and training, spare parts (burned through in wartime), compatible munitions and deep maintenance.
BAE employees on the ground in Saudi Arabia
“In every practical way short of engaging in combat.”
Early boasts of a “lightning operation” went quiet once it became a quagmire and the bombing of civilians was documented. “Not combatants” sounds like a Foreign Office lawyer’s word.
Reports of British special forces in a Saudi-led ground offensive (2017) and questions over targeting were always played down.
Withdraw support and the jets are grounded within weeks: no ammunition, no maintenance, no parts.
“I don’t want to overstate British agency, but I don’t think we should understate it either.”
leaves.c: Under Obama, a British pull-out could have forced Washington to take notice

leaves.x: British complicity runs far deeper than in Gaza: “nothing like” it.
An air-and-sea blockade of the region’s poorest, import-dependent country. Its consequences were foreseeable: “a fair indication that you intended it.”
Ports, airports, roads and cranes; weddings, funerals, hospitals and schools. It destroyed the essential means of life.
Strikes on farms and fishing boats. Mwatana’s report Starvation Makers found both sides used starvation as a method of warfare.
Free-fire zones in the north abolished distinction, a core principle of international law.
infants dead of starvation or disease in the early years (Save the Children)
total deaths (UNDP), around half from hunger and disease
civilians killed in coalition air raids
A historic cholera outbreak; the UN called it “the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.” The Houthis also besieged enemy-held cities, but the coalition was the leading culprit.
of human development reversed (UNDP, 2019)
Not identical to Gaza, but collective punishment, denial of the means of survival and indiscriminate bombing are all there. It belongs “in the same breath as Iraq, Syria, Gaza, Sudan.”
arms licensed to Saudi Arabia, Jan–Apr 2026, most likely air-to-surface missiles
UK military advisers, plus an RAF Voyager tanker from the Burnham government for “Saudi defensive activity.”
Licensing is opaque, giving only a category and a value. Nothing else in that category is worth that much except “a big pile of bombs.” Restocking for now?
“A shield is a weapon.”
leaves.c: Defensive cover gives a known war criminal impunity, and more incentive to strike

leaves.x: Is “defensive only” in writing? If not, why not? How is it monitored? What happens if they don’t comply?
Refuelling one sortie that hits a hospital is not “small beer.” Saudi silence and no independent reporting, against seven years of proof.
It is the same lawyerly line as the RAF bases lent to US jets in the war on Iran. In 2024–25 the UK also joined US strikes on Yemen.
Prime contractor under government-to-government deals. Saudi Arabia is historically its third-largest customer.
Co-produces the Tornado and Typhoon engines, the major secondary actor.
BAE revenue from the Saudi MoD, 2015–22 (≥ £2.3bn every year)
war profits: BAE £3.56bn + Rolls-Royce £0.33bn
They knew from day one. Amnesty reported within a week, Amnesty and HRW within months, and UN experts by early 2016: “widespread, systematic.”
“Zero sympathy” for “it’s for the government to judge.”
leaves.c: Licensed or not, the profits should be confiscated

leaves.x: CAAT’s court cases could only test whether Whitehall’s process was rational, never whether Saudi Arabia broke international law.

Lost, then won on appeal (2019): key evidence had been ignored and licences were suspended. After its “homework” Whitehall called the violations “isolated incidents” and sales resumed. A new challenge was lost.
“Atrocity after atrocity after atrocity.”
leaves.c: A summer spent reading every UN and NGO report for his forthcoming book

leaves.x: Confiscate the arms firms’ war profits, an indicative £3.9bn from open sources. A government could calculate it precisely.
Britain’s state shares the guilt; it isn’t in it only for arms profits. Match the £3.9bn from an aid budget restored to 0.7% of GNI.
total reparations: humanitarian relief first, then a Yemeni reconstruction fund
Aid fell from 0.7% of GNI (met from 2013) to 0.5% under the Tories in 2021, and to 0.3% under Starmer by 2027, to pay for the military. Restoring 0.7% means about £21.5bn.
“It shouldn’t be aid, it should be reparations.”
leaves.c: The offhand remark, a year ago, that became the report

leaves.x: UN humanitarian shortfall for Yemen, January 2026
In international law, a state that aids a wrongful act owes reparation (Mwatana and Yale, Returned to Zero, 2022).
Also: a full arms embargo on the coalition states, and on Israel and the suppliers of Sudan’s RSF.
Spread it: US activists, then France and Germany. Use reparations as a lever for diplomacy, and set a precedent against war profiteering.
Britain as a benign force: “a kind of national religion.”
leaves.c: A BBC One debate guest “proud” of UK aid to Yemen, at the height of the bombing

leaves.x: Aid debates assume munificence. Even the “progressive” line is “be more generous,” not “stop causing harm.”
The Israel-lobby thesis (Mearsheimer and Walt) is a realist, centre-right theory that casts the state as innocent and corrupted from outside. Britain “doesn’t need to be corrupted.”
“You’re not going to be surprised by Britain’s role in Gaza if you’ve been following what Britain did in Yemen.”
24 unarmed civilians killed by the Scots Guards in Malaya. No charges, no apology, no redress.
Caroline Elkins’s “gulag.” Testimony and hidden archives forced an out-of-court settlement: small sums, but an admission.
Collective punishment keeps recurring: make the population’s life hell to turn it against the rebels.
A long shot under Burnham or Miliband. Even so, the campaign puts British militarism under the microscope and builds pressure from below.
Premier League charges reportedly upheld against UAE-owned Manchester City
Relegate them to Manchester League Division Five, and fine them the GDP of Abu Dhabi.
Football is a vast British cultural export, “vandalised” by cheating. A decade of it now feels fake, and rivals were cheated of titles and Champions League places.
Gulf owners came for hard-headed reasons: to insulate the UK government from pressure from below.
Local investment in Manchester and Newcastle builds a domestic constituency that would resist any break with Riyadh or Abu Dhabi.
The old playbook was quiet: property and shareholdings kept below the ~15% that brings attention.
The spotlight cuts both ways. Even apolitical football podcasts discussed human rights during Qatar 2022.
“The biggest scandal in English football history.”
leaves.c: Monarchies used to impunity at home misjudge institutions abroad
